name: Smithfield Weekly Market
notes: Drovers arrive Sunday night before Monday market. Defoe (1724-26): without question the greatest market in the world. Average 74000 cattle and 570000 sheep per year 1740-1750. Animal waste deposited in surrounding streets.
sources: Defoe Tour 1724-26; White London in the Eighteenth Century 2012; Museum of London Sensory Smithfield Report 2017

name: Billingsgate Fish Market
notes: Act passed in 1699 (often cited under 1698 regnal dating) made Billingsgate a free and open market for fish. Six-day fish market with a separate Sunday mackerel exception not modelled here. Opens c.05:00. Language of Billingsgate a byword for abuse from at least the 18th century.
sources: City of London official history; Billingsgate Act 1698 (10 & 11 Will. III c.24; 4 May 1699); White 2012

name: Leadenhall Market
sources: Old and New London British History Online; Porter London A Social History 1994

name: Covent Garden Market
notes: Charter 1670 for Tue/Thu/Sat. Busiest c.06:00; costermongers surround market. No later than 09:00. Malcolm Thick documents the Neat House Gardens hinterland supplying this market.
sources: Old and New London British History Online; Thick Neat House Gardens 1998

name: Bartholomew Fair
notes: Pre-1752: Aug 24 OS. Post-1752: Sep 3 NS (calendar reform exemption). Originally 3 days; by 18th c. ~14 days in practice though officially 4. Cloth/livestock fair became sideshows/entertainment. Suppressed 1855.
sources: Old and New London British History Online vol.2; History Today; Wikipedia

name: Southwark Fair
notes: Charter 1462 for Sep 7-9 but expanded to ~2 weeks. City repeatedly tried to restrict. Suppressed Jun 22 1762; last fair 1763 forcibly cleared. Hogarth painted it 1733.
sources: Georgian Cities Sorbonne; Past Tense London History; Hogarth Southwark Fair 1733

name: May Fair
notes: First two weeks of May. Suppressed c.1708 when site became residential Mayfair.

name: Greenwich Fair
notes: Twice-yearly Easter and Whitsun fair. Tumbling down Observatory Hill a central attraction. Associated with pickpocketing gambling and drunkenness. Suppressed in 1857 for rowdiness; the precise movable feast dates are not modelled in this schema.
sources: Friends of Greenwich Park; The Genealogist

name: Thames Frost Fair
notes: Occurs only in severe winters. See event_instances for specific dates. Booths printing presses horse racing on ice. Last fair 1814; Thames embankment ended conditions for future fairs.
sources: Andrews Famous Frosts and Frost Fairs 1887 Project Gutenberg

name: Tyburn Hanging Day
notes: Approx 8 times per year almost always Monday. 10000-50000 crowd for celebrity executions. Procession from Newgate took up to 3 hours. Bell of St Sepulchre's rang only on hanging days. Last execution Nov 3 1783.
sources: Linebaugh London Hanged 1992; Gatrell Hanging Tree 1994; Capital Punishment UK; Old Bailey Online Journey from Newgate to Tyburn

name: Newgate Gallows Execution
notes: Post-1783 executions outside Newgate Prison. More frequent than Tyburn; smaller crowds but concentrated.

name: Tyburn Procession Route
notes: The 3-mile route from Newgate through Holborn and St Giles to Oxford Street. Crowds lined the route.
sources: Old Bailey Online Journey from Newgate to Tyburn

name: Vauxhall Gardens Season
notes: Late May to September. Originally open nightly in season; Saturdays were discontinued in 1806 after late-night disorder and the gardens were thereafter usually open only three nights a week. 1s admission from 1732. Water features and walks were part of the designed atmosphere.
sources: Coke and Borg Vauxhall Gardens A History Yale UP 2011; Wroth The London Pleasure Gardens of the Eighteenth Century

name: Ranelagh Gardens Season
notes: Season from Easter into August. Usually open Mondays Wednesdays and Fridays; evening concerts began around 6:30 or 7. Half-crown admission included tea coffee and bread and butter. Closed 1803; Rotunda demolished 1805.
sources: Parks and Gardens UK; Wroth The London Pleasure Gardens of the Eighteenth Century

name: Marylebone Gardens Season
notes: Spring to autumn season. Closed 1778 when site was developed for housing.

name: Lord Mayor's Show
notes: Pre-1752: Oct 28 (Feast of St Simon and St Jude). Post-1752: Nov 9 to preserve the mayoral year after calendar reform. Route varied annually through the new Mayor's ward; the procession conveyed the Lord Mayor from the City to Westminster to swear loyalty to the Crown.
sources: Lord Mayor's Show dates and routes; City of London History of the City in Ten Documents

name: Gunpowder Plot Celebrations
notes: Nov 5. Bell-ringing bonfires forced illumination of houses. Contested: Tory/Whig/Dissenter communities experienced differently. Corbin: bells shaped the habitus of a community imparting depth to the desire for rootedness.
sources: Corbin Village Bells Columbia UP 1998; Rogers Crowds Culture and Politics 1998

name: Handel Commemoration Concerts
notes: Five concerts marking supposed centenary of Handel's death (misdated). Greatest musical event of the century per contemporaries. Westminster Abbey and Pantheon. Hoock: combined sensual impact of sights and sounds left strong impressions.
sources: Hoock Empires of the Imagination Profile Books 2010; Burney research notes

name: Gordon Riots
notes: June 2-9 1780. Anti-Catholic riots. Crowds rang bells upon arrival. Forced illumination of houses. Chapels and Catholic houses attacked. Rogers: legitimacy of political regimes intimately bound up with the way crowds intervened in public space.
sources: Rogers Crowds Culture and Politics Oxford UP 1998; Burney research notes Ch.5
